title: Generic matrix-group laws extend to scheme-theoretic closure
statement: Let $F$ be a field [def-weil-field], $E$ a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space, and $G\subseteq\operatorname{GL}(E)$ an affine finite-type closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup, def-sc-general-linear-group]; in dimension zero put $\operatorname{GL}(0)=1$. Let $C=\operatorname{Spec}A$ be an affine finite-type $F$-scheme such that $A\otimes_F L$ is a nonzero integral domain for every field extension $L/F$. Let $j:C\to G$ be a quasi-compact immersion, that is, a closed immersion followed by an open immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-weil-open-immersion], and suppose there is $c_0\in C(F)$ with $j(c_0)=1$. Suppose there are nonempty opens $V\subseteq C\times_F C$ and $W\subseteq C$ and morphisms $m_0:V\to C$, $i_0:W\to C$ satisfying $j\circ m_0=m_G\circ(j\times j)|_V$ and $j\circ i_0=i_G\circ j|_W$, where $m_G$ and $i_G$ are multiplication and inversion in $G$. Put $B=\Gamma(G,\mathcal O_G)$ and $I=\ker(j^*:B\to A)$. Then multiplication, inverse and identity of $G$ restrict to the closed subscheme $H=\operatorname{Spec}(B/I)$, making $H\hookrightarrow G$ a closed subgroup scheme. In particular this $H$ is the scheme-theoretic image of $j$ [def-nagata-scheme-theoretic-image]. Neither a group law on all of $C$, nor smoothness of $G$ or $C$, is assumed.

source.place: Section 1c, Lemma 1.40 and Theorem 1.45, printed pp.18-19, closure stability argument; agent generalization to an affine locus with only generic multiplication and inversion, proved by the coordinate-kernel/tensor-injection argument recorded in report.md.

proof.text: Write $r=j^*:B\to A$, $D=B/I$, $q:B\to D$, and $p:D\hookrightarrow A$, $p(q(b))=r(b)$. The formula for $p$ is well defined and injective since $I=\ker r$ [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. The affine group coordinate theorem [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf] supplies the pullbacks $\Delta:B\to B\otimes_F B$, $S:B\to B$ and $\epsilon:B\to F$ of the given multiplication, inverse and identity. Identify $C\times_F C$ with $\operatorname{Spec}(A\otimes_F A)$ by [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra].

source.place: Section 1c, Lemma 1.40 and Theorem 1.45, printed pp.18-19; agent coordinate-kernel proof for the generic-law variant (not an invocation of the rational-point closure theorem).

proof.text: The algebra $A$ is a nonzero domain by the hypothesis at $L=F$. Put $K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)$. Tensor the injection $A\hookrightarrow K$ with the $F$-vector space $A$: [lem-weil-pbc-module-over-field-flat] and [lem-trf-flat-tensor-preserves-injection] give an injection $A\otimes_F A\hookrightarrow A\otimes_F K$. Its target is a nonzero domain by the hypothesis at $L=K$, so its unital subring $A\otimes_F A$ is a nonzero domain. Thus $C$ and $C\times_F C$ are integral schemes [def-pc-integral-scheme]. For clarity, the affine criterion follows directly from this definition: an affine open in the spectrum of a domain is covered by principal opens whose rings are domain localizations, and its sections embed in the common fraction field.

source.place: Section 1c, Lemma 1.40 and Theorem 1.45, printed pp.18-19; agent coordinate-kernel proof for the generic-law variant (not an invocation of the rational-point closure theorem).

proof.text: Tensoring $p:D\hookrightarrow A$ first with $D$ and then with $A$ preserves injectivity, since both are $F$-vector spaces [lem-weil-pbc-module-over-field-flat, lem-trf-flat-tensor-preserves-injection]. Consequently $p\otimes p:D\otimes_F D\hookrightarrow A\otimes_F A$ is injective. For $b\in I$, the section $(r\otimes r)\Delta(b)$ restricts on $V$ to $m_0^*(r(b))=0$ by the stated equality of morphisms. Choose a point $v\in V$. Its germ is zero; the injectivity of the germ map for an integral scheme [lem-sc-integral-scheme-stalks-in-function-field], applied to the global open of $C\times_F C$, gives $(r\otimes r)\Delta(b)=0$. Hence injectivity of $p\otimes p$ gives $(q\otimes q)\Delta(b)=0$.

source.place: Section 1c, Lemma 1.40 and Theorem 1.45, printed pp.18-19; agent coordinate-kernel proof for the generic-law variant (not an invocation of the rational-point closure theorem).

proof.text: Likewise, for $b\in I$, $r(S(b))$ restricts on $W$ to $i_0^*(r(b))=0$. Choose $w\in W$ and apply the injective germ map of the integral scheme $C$ [lem-sc-integral-scheme-stalks-in-function-field]. Thus $r(S(b))=0$, so $S(b)\in I$. Also $\epsilon(b)=c_0^*(r(b))=0$, since $j(c_0)=1$. This proves that $qS$ and $\epsilon$ kill $I$, in addition to the vanishing of $(q\otimes q)\Delta$ on $I$ from step 3.

source.place: Section 1c, Lemma 1.40 and Theorem 1.45, printed pp.18-19; agent coordinate-kernel proof for the generic-law variant (not an invocation of the rational-point closure theorem).

proof.text: Define $\Delta_D(q(b))=(q\otimes q)\Delta(b)$, $S_D(q(b))=q(S(b))$, and $\epsilon_D(q(b))=\epsilon(b)$. Steps 3 and 4 make these formulas independent of the representative $b$; they are $F$-algebra maps because their composites with the surjective $q$ are $F$-algebra maps [def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. By the contravariant affine spectrum correspondence [def-weil-affine-spectrum] and the affine product identification [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-product-affine-spectra], they give actual morphisms $H\times_F H\to H$, $H\to H$ and $\operatorname{Spec}F\to H$. Their composites with $h=\operatorname{Spec}q:H\to G$ are the restrictions of the specified operations on $G$, by the three displayed coordinate equalities. The surjectivity of $q$ makes $h$ a closed immersion [def-weil-closed-immersion].

source.place: Section 1c, Lemma 1.40 and Theorem 1.45, printed pp.18-19; agent coordinate-kernel proof for the generic-law variant (not an invocation of the rational-point closure theorem).

proof.text: For every commutative $F$-algebra $R$, precomposition with the surjection $q$ injects $\operatorname{Hom}_{F\text{-alg}}(D,R)$ into $\operatorname{Hom}_{F\text{-alg}}(B,R)$. The morphisms of step 5 show that its image contains the identity and is closed under the multiplication and inverse of $G(R)$. It is therefore a subgroup, and its group identities are precisely the identities inherited from $G(R)$. The functor-of-points formulation of [def-sc-group-scheme] now makes these morphisms a group-scheme structure on $H$, and [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] says that the closed immersion $h$ is a closed subgroup scheme. This argument verifies the identities on all test algebras, including nonreduced ones.

source.place: Section 1c, Lemma 1.40 and Theorem 1.45, printed pp.18-19; agent coordinate-kernel proof for the generic-law variant (not an invocation of the rational-point closure theorem).

proof.text: Finally $r=pq$ factors $j$ through $H$. Every closed subscheme $Z\hookrightarrow G=\operatorname{Spec}B$ is $\operatorname{Spec}(B/J)$ for an ideal $J\subseteq B$ [def-weil-closed-immersion]. By the affine spectrum correspondence [def-weil-affine-spectrum], $j$ factors through $Z$ exactly when $J\subseteq\ker r=I$: a map killing $J$ descends by $b+J\mapsto r(b)$, and a factorization kills $J$. In that case $B/J\to B/I$ gives a unique comparison $H\to Z$ over $G$. Thus $H$ is the smallest closed subscheme through which $j$ factors, which is the scheme-theoretic image by [lemma-nagata-scheme-theoretic-closure-minimal, def-nagata-scheme-theoretic-image]. None of these steps requires smoothness or an everywhere-defined law on $C$.
